glance.label: Main Idea
glance.html: Pharaoh answers the LORD’s demand with “Who is the LORD, that I should obey His voice?” and crushes the call to worship under heavier labor, leaving Israel’s officers bitter and Moses pouring out his distress to the God who sent him.

glance.label: Setting
glance.html: Exodus 5 follows directly on Israel’s worship in 4:31. Moses and Aaron now stand before Pharaoh for the first time, as the LORD had warned that Pharaoh would refuse (3:19; 4:21).

glance.label: Chapter Outline
glance.html:
• Exodus 5:1–5 — Pharaoh Refuses to Know the LORD

  • Exodus 5:6–14 — Pharaoh Withholds the Straw and Increases the Burden

  • Exodus 5:15–21 — The Officers Appeal to Pharaoh and Blame Moses and Aaron

  • Exodus 5:22–23 — Moses Brings His Distress to the LORD

glance.label: Key Verse
glance.html: “And Pharaoh said, ‘Who is the LORD, that I should obey His voice to let Israel go? I do not know the LORD, nor will I let Israel go.’” (Exodus 5:2)

cards.title: The Heart of the Chapter
cards.html:
Moses and Aaron bring the LORD’s word: “Let My people go, that they may hold a feast to Me in the wilderness” (5:1). The LORD claims Israel as His own and calls them to worship. Pharaoh’s reply sets the question the next ten chapters will answer: “Who is the LORD, that I should obey His voice to let Israel go? I do not know the LORD” (5:2). The real dispute is over who has the right to Israel’s service.

Pharaoh answers with policy. He withholds the straw but keeps the brick quota, calls the people “idle,” and dismisses God’s call as “false words” (5:9). Harder labor is meant to silence the desire to worship. The people scatter across Egypt for stubble, their officers are beaten, and the hope of chapter 4 turns to blame. The officers accuse Moses and Aaron of putting a sword in Pharaoh’s hand. Moses has nowhere to take that accusation but to the LORD, and he takes it honestly: “Why is it You have sent me?” (5:22). The chapter ends with no relief yet. God’s answer begins in the next verse of the story.

cards.title: Chapter Sections
cards.html:
Exodus 5:1–5 — Pharaoh Refuses to Know the LORD

Moses and Aaron deliver the LORD’s command to let His people go and worship Him. Pharaoh refuses to acknowledge the LORD at all, sends them back to work, and complains that they are giving the people rest.

Exodus 5:6–14 — Pharaoh Withholds the Straw and Increases the Burden

That same day Pharaoh orders that the people gather their own straw while making the same number of bricks, calling their desire to sacrifice laziness. Israel scatters through Egypt for stubble, and their officers are beaten when the quota is not met.

Exodus 5:15–21 — The Officers Appeal to Pharaoh and Blame Moses and Aaron

The officers appeal to Pharaoh, but he only repeats, “You are idle! Idle!” (5:17), and holds them to the full quota. Leaving the palace, they turn on Moses and Aaron and blame them for making Israel hateful to Pharaoh.

Exodus 5:22–23 — Moses Brings His Distress to the LORD

Moses returns to the LORD and asks why He has brought trouble on His people and why He sent Moses at all. Since Moses spoke in God’s name, things have only grown worse, and the people have not yet been delivered.

cards.title: Why This Chapter Matters
cards.html:
Exodus 5 exposes what Pharaoh’s power is for. He calls the people idle and increases their work so that they will not regard what he calls false words (5:8–9). The oppression is aimed at keeping God’s people too exhausted to answer God’s call. Pharaoh’s question, “Who is the LORD?” is answered as the plagues unfold, when Egypt learns “that I am the LORD” (7:5).

The chapter is honest about what obedience can cost. Moses obeyed, and things got worse. Scripture does not hide the gap between God’s promise and the people’s circumstances, and it shows Moses bringing his confusion straight to God. Obedience does not guarantee quick relief, but God can be trusted with the hardest questions about His timing.

cards.title: Key Themes to Watch For
cards.html:
Who commands Israel’s service. The LORD claims Israel as His people for worship, while Pharaoh claims them for his labor (5:1–5).

Knowing the LORD. Pharaoh says, “I do not know the LORD” (5:2), the challenge the rest of the plague story answers.

Oppression that silences worship. Heavier labor is meant to crush the people’s cry to sacrifice to God (5:8–9, 17).

Honest prayer under pressure. Moses brings the officers’ accusation and his own distress to the LORD (5:22–23).

cards.title: Key Words & Concepts
cards.html:
Feast to Me in the wilderness (5:1). A festival of worship to the LORD away from Egypt. From the start, the goal of Israel’s release is worship.

Three days’ journey (5:3). The distance Israel asks to travel to sacrifice. The request tested whether Pharaoh would honor the LORD’s basic claim on His people.

Straw and stubble (5:7, 12). Straw was mixed into mud bricks. Forcing the people to gather their own stubble made the same quota nearly impossible.

Officers (5:14). Israelite foremen set over their own people by Pharaoh’s taskmasters. They are beaten when the quota is not met.

outline: Exodus 5:1–5 — Pharaoh Refuses to Know the LORD
Exodus 5:6–14 — Pharaoh Withholds the Straw and Increases the Burden
Exodus 5:15–21 — The Officers Appeal to Pharaoh and Blame Moses and Aaron
Exodus 5:22–23 — Moses Brings His Distress to the LORD

focus: Exodus 5 records Pharaoh’s first answer to the LORD’s demand: he refuses to acknowledge the LORD and makes Israel’s labor harder to crush their call to worship. The chapter moves from the palace to the brickfields and back to Pharaoh, then shows the beaten officers turning on Moses and Moses taking his distress to the LORD.

sections.title: Pharaoh Refuses to Know the LORD
sections.summary: Moses and Aaron deliver the LORD’s word, “Let My people go, that they may hold a feast to Me in the wilderness” (Exodus 5:1), and Pharaoh answers, “Who is the LORD, that I should obey His voice” (Exodus 5:2). When they plead for a three days’ journey to sacrifice, Pharaoh orders them back to work and complains that they make the people rest.

sections.title: Pharaoh Withholds the Straw and Increases the Burden
sections.summary: The same day Pharaoh commands that the people gather their own straw while making the same quota of bricks, calling their desire to sacrifice idleness. The people scatter through Egypt to gather stubble, and the Israelite officers are beaten when the quota is not met.

sections.title: The Officers Appeal to Pharaoh and Blame Moses and Aaron
sections.summary: The officers cry out to Pharaoh, but he repeats, “You are idle! Idle!” (Exodus 5:17), and holds them to the full quota. Coming out from Pharaoh, they meet Moses and Aaron and accuse them of making Israel abhorrent to Pharaoh and putting a sword in his hand to kill them.

sections.title: Moses Brings His Distress to the LORD
sections.summary: Moses returns to the LORD and asks, “Lord, why have You brought trouble on this people? Why is it You have sent me?” (Exodus 5:22). Since he spoke in the LORD’s name, Pharaoh has done evil to the people, and the LORD has not yet delivered them.

1.brief: Moses and Aaron go to Pharaoh with the LORD’s word: “Let My people go, that they may hold a feast to Me in the wilderness.” The LORD claims Israel as His own people and calls them to worship Him.
1.explain:
“Afterward Moses and Aaron went in and told Pharaoh,”

After the elders believed and worshiped (4:29–31), Moses and Aaron took God’s message to the palace. Moses, who had spent years tending sheep in Midian (3:1), and his brother Aaron walked in to address the most powerful king of their world.

“Thus says the LORD God of Israel:”

They spoke with a prophet’s formula. These were not their words but the words of “the LORD God of Israel.” Pharaoh was used to being treated as divine. Now he heard a command from a God he did not acknowledge.

“Let My people go, that they may hold a feast to Me in the wilderness.”

God calls Israel “My people.” They were Pharaoh’s slaves, but they belonged to the LORD. The purpose of their release was worship: to “hold a feast,” a sacred festival in God’s honor. The whole conflict of the next chapters turns on one question: who has the right to Israel’s service?
1.notes: The Hebrew verb behind “hold a feast” refers to celebrating a pilgrimage festival. Later Israel would keep three such feasts each year (23:14–17).

2.brief: Pharaoh answers, “Who is the LORD, that I should obey His voice to let Israel go?” and declares that he does not know the LORD and will not let Israel go. He refuses to acknowledge the LORD’s right to command him, and the rest of the plague story answers his question.
2.explain:
“And Pharaoh said, ‘Who is the LORD, that I should obey His voice to let Israel go?”

Pharaoh’s reply is contempt. He does not ask in order to learn. He asks to dismiss. In his eyes, the God of a nation of slaves had no claim on Egypt’s king. The rest of the plague story answers his question. By the end, Egypt will know exactly who the LORD is (7:5; 14:4, 18).

“I do not know the LORD, nor will I let Israel go.”

Pharaoh says plainly that he does not know the LORD and will not release His people. The two refusals go together. Because he would not acknowledge the LORD, he would not obey Him. To know the LORD in Exodus is more than knowing about Him. It is recognizing His authority. Pharaoh refuses both.
2.notes: Throughout the plague narrative, the LORD’s acts show Pharaoh and Egypt who He is: that He is the LORD (7:17), that there is no one like Him (8:10; 9:14), that He is the LORD in the midst of the land (8:22), and that the earth is His (9:29). The first of these reads, “By this you shall know that I am the LORD” (7:17). Pharaoh’s “I do not know the LORD” sets up that theme.

3.brief: Moses and Aaron explain that the God of the Hebrews has met with them and ask to go three days’ journey to sacrifice, lest He strike them with pestilence or the sword. They present the request as a matter of obedience to their God.
3.explain:
“So they said, ‘The God of the Hebrews has met with us.”

Moses and Aaron answer without anger. They explain that “the God of the Hebrews” has met with them. They name God by His relationship with the despised people Pharaoh ruled.

“Please, let us go three days’ journey into the desert and sacrifice to the LORD our God,”

They repeat the modest request God had given them (3:18): a three-day journey into the desert to offer sacrifice. They ask politely, with the word “Please.”

“lest He fall upon us with pestilence or with the sword.”

They add a reason: failing to obey their God would be dangerous. He might strike them with “pestilence,” disease, or “the sword,” violence. They present the request as a matter of obedience to their God, and they speak of His judgment as falling on them, not on Pharaoh.

4.brief: The king asks why Moses and Aaron are taking the people from their work and orders them back to their labor. Pharaoh treats the call to worship as an interruption of Egypt’s work.
4.explain:
“Then the king of Egypt said to them, ‘Moses and Aaron, why do you take the people from their work?”

Pharaoh answers as a slave master. He calls the brothers by name and accuses them of distracting the people from “their work.” In his view, Israel existed to serve Egypt. A call to worship was simply an interruption.

“Get back to your labor.”

Pharaoh dismisses Moses and Aaron with an order to get back to work. He treats the whole matter as a labor dispute.
4.notes: The Hebrew word translated “labor” here means burdens or forced labor. It is the same word translated “burdens” in 1:11 and 2:11.

5.brief: Pharaoh complains that the people of the land are now many and that Moses and Aaron are making them rest from their labor. To Pharaoh, Israel’s value lies only in their work for Egypt.
5.explain:
“And Pharaoh said, ‘Look, the people of the land are many now,”

Pharaoh notes how numerous the Israelites have become. The growth that alarmed an earlier king (1:9) is now a workforce Egypt depends on.

“and you make them rest from their labor!”

To Pharaoh, a three-day journey for worship meant lost labor. The word “rest” is related to the word for Sabbath. Pharaoh resents any interruption of their work. To him, Israel’s value lies only in their work for Egypt.
5.notes: The Hebrew verb translated “make them rest” is the verb from which the word “Sabbath” comes. Later God would give Israel a weekly day of rest (16:23–30; 20:8–11).

6.brief: On that same day Pharaoh gives orders to the taskmasters and the Israelite officers. His response to the request is immediate and harsh.
6.explain:
“So the same day Pharaoh commanded the taskmasters of the people and their officers, saying,”

Pharaoh acts “the same day.” His response is immediate and harsh. He gives orders to two groups: “the taskmasters,” Egyptian overseers, and “their officers,” Israelite foremen who were responsible for their fellow workers (5:14).
6.notes: The Hebrew word translated “officers” likely refers to scribes or recordkeepers who tracked the brick quotas.

7.brief: Pharaoh orders that the people no longer be given straw to make bricks and must gather straw for themselves. The work becomes much harder without any reduction in what is demanded.
7.explain:
“You shall no longer give the people straw to make brick as before.”

Straw was mixed into mud bricks to strengthen them and keep them from cracking as they dried. Until now, the Egyptians had supplied it. Pharaoh orders that it no longer be given.

“Let them go and gather straw for themselves.”

The people must now find their own straw. The work becomes much harder without any reduction in what is demanded.

8.brief: The people must still make the same quota of bricks, because Pharaoh says they are idle and that is why they cry out to go and sacrifice to their God. He mocks the desire to worship as laziness.
8.explain:
“And you shall lay on them the quota of bricks which they made before. You shall not reduce it.”

The daily quota stays the same. The people must produce as many bricks as before while also gathering the materials themselves.

“For they are idle; therefore they cry out, saying, ‘Let us go and sacrifice to our God.”

Pharaoh explains his reasoning. He calls the people “idle,” lazy. In his view, only people with too much time on their hands would talk about worship. He mocks the desire to worship as laziness.

9.brief: Pharaoh commands that more work be laid on the men so they will labor and “not regard false words.” He uses heavier labor to silence the LORD’s call, which he dismisses as lies.
9.explain:
“Let more work be laid on the men, that they may labor in it,”

Pharaoh’s answer to the request for worship is more work. Exhausted people have no strength to think about anything else.

“and let them not regard false words.”

Pharaoh calls God’s message “false words,” lies. He uses heavier labor to silence the LORD’s call. If the people are worked hard enough, they will stop listening to Moses.
9.notes: The Hebrew verb translated “regard” means to look to or pay attention to. Pharaoh wants to crush the people’s attention to God’s promise.

10.brief: The taskmasters and officers go out and tell the people that Pharaoh will no longer give them straw. Pharaoh’s order now falls on the whole people.
10.explain:
“And the taskmasters of the people and their officers went out and spoke to the people, saying,”

The Egyptian overseers and the Israelite officers go out to announce the new order. The officers now have to carry Pharaoh’s command to their own people.

“Thus says Pharaoh: ‘I will not give you straw.”

The announcement begins with a phrase that sounds like a prophet’s formula: “Thus says Pharaoh.” Moses had come with “Thus says the LORD” (5:1). Now Pharaoh answers with his own word. The two claims to Israel’s service stand side by side. Pharaoh’s order now falls on the whole people.

11.brief: The people must gather straw wherever they can find it, yet none of their work will be reduced. The new burden is meant to crush them.
11.explain:
“Go, get yourselves straw where you can find it;”

The people must find straw wherever they can.

“yet none of your work will be reduced.”

The burden is increased while the quota stays fixed. The new demand is meant to crush them.

12.brief: The people scatter throughout Egypt to gather stubble instead of straw. The order drives Israel across the land in search of materials.
12.explain:
“So the people were scattered abroad throughout all the land of Egypt to gather stubble instead of straw.”

The people scattered across Egypt looking for materials. They gathered “stubble,” the stalks left in the fields after harvest, because proper straw was not available. The work became slower and harder. The order drove Israel across the land in search of materials.
12.notes: The Hebrew word translated “stubble” refers to the short stalks left standing after grain was cut. It made poorer material than chopped straw.

13.brief: The taskmasters press them to hurry and to fulfill their daily quota as when straw was supplied. The demand ignores the impossible conditions the people now face.
13.explain:
“And the taskmasters forced them to hurry, saying, ‘Fulfill your work, your daily quota, as when there was straw.”

The taskmasters pressed the people to work faster. They demanded the same daily quota as before. The demand ignored the impossible conditions the people now faced.

14.brief: The Israelite officers whom the taskmasters had set over the people are beaten and asked why they have not met the brick quota. The cruelty falls on the Israelite leaders who stand between the taskmasters and the people.
14.explain:
“Also the officers of the children of Israel, whom Pharaoh’s taskmasters had set over them, were beaten”

The Israelite officers were held responsible for the shortfall, and they were “beaten.” The cruelty fell on the Israelite leaders who stood between the taskmasters and the people.

“and were asked, ‘Why have you not fulfilled your task in making brick both yesterday and today, as before?”

The question demanded an explanation that the taskmasters already knew. There was no straw. The question was part of the abuse.

15.brief: The officers of Israel come and cry out to Pharaoh, “Why are you dealing thus with your servants?” They appeal to Pharaoh himself for justice.
15.explain:
“Then the officers of the children of Israel came and cried out to Pharaoh, saying,”

The officers went over the heads of the taskmasters and “cried out to Pharaoh.” They hoped the king would see the injustice and correct it.

“Why are you dealing thus with your servants?”

They called themselves “your servants.” They appealed to Pharaoh for fair treatment. They did not appeal to God. Their hope was still in Egypt’s king.
15.notes: A closely related verb is used for Israel’s cry to God in 2:23. Here the cry goes to Pharaoh.

16.brief: The officers explain that no straw is given, yet they are told to make bricks and are beaten, though the fault lies with Pharaoh’s own people. They point out that the failure is not theirs.
16.explain:
“There is no straw given to your servants, and they say to us, ‘Make brick!”

The officers describe the impossible situation. They are given no straw, yet they are ordered to make bricks.

“And indeed your servants are beaten, but the fault is in your own people.”

They are punished, but the fault is not theirs. It lies with Pharaoh’s own officials, who set an impossible quota. The officers point out that the failure is not theirs.
16.notes: The final clause is difficult in Hebrew. The NKJV reads “the fault is in your own people.” Other renderings understand it to mean that Pharaoh is wronging his own people, meaning that Pharaoh wrongs the Israelites who serve him.

17.brief: Pharaoh answers, “You are idle! Idle!” and says that is why they ask to go and sacrifice to the LORD. He repeats his accusation and refuses to hear their complaint.
17.explain:
“But he said, ‘You are idle! Idle!”

Pharaoh repeats the word for emphasis. He does not hear the complaint. He simply repeats his accusation.

“Therefore you say, ‘Let us go and sacrifice to the LORD.”

Pharaoh ties the request to worship to their supposed laziness. In his eyes, the request to sacrifice to “the LORD” is only an excuse for idleness.

18.brief: Pharaoh tells them to go back to work, for no straw will be given, yet they must deliver the full quota of bricks. The appeal only confirms the harsh order.
18.explain:
“Therefore go now and work; for no straw shall be given you,”

Pharaoh sends them back to work. Nothing has changed. There will still be no straw.

“yet you shall deliver the quota of bricks.”

The full quota remains. The appeal only confirms the harsh order.

19.brief: The officers see that they are in trouble when they are told they must not reduce the daily quota. Their situation now looks hopeless.
19.explain:
“And the officers of the children of Israel saw that they were in trouble after it was said,”

The officers understood that their situation was desperate. The phrase “in trouble” means in an evil or hopeless position.

“You shall not reduce any bricks from your daily quota.”

The order left no room for relief. They could not meet it, and they would be beaten for failing. Their situation now looked hopeless.

20.brief: As they come out from Pharaoh, the officers meet Moses and Aaron, who are waiting for them. The scene turns from Pharaoh to the men who brought God’s message.
20.explain:
“Then, as they came out from Pharaoh, they met Moses and Aaron who stood there to meet them.”

As the officers left the palace, they found Moses and Aaron waiting. The brothers had evidently come to hear the outcome. The scene turns from Pharaoh to the men who brought God’s message.

21.brief: The Israelite officers say, “Let the LORD look on you and judge,” accusing Moses and Aaron of making Israel hateful to Pharaoh and giving him a sword to kill them. The hope that greeted Moses’ message in Exodus 4:31 has turned to blame among the officers who bear Pharaoh’s punishment.
21.explain:
“And they said to them, ‘Let the LORD look on you and judge,”

The officers turn on Moses and Aaron. They call on the LORD to judge the brothers for what they have done. They use God’s name against God’s messengers.

“because you have made us abhorrent in the sight of Pharaoh and in the sight of his servants,”

They accuse Moses and Aaron of making them “abhorrent,” literally making them stink, in the eyes of Pharaoh and his officials.

“to put a sword in their hand to kill us.”

They believe the brothers have given Pharaoh a weapon to destroy them. The hope that greeted Moses’ message in 4:31 has turned to blame among the officers who bear Pharaoh’s punishment.
21.notes: The Hebrew phrase translated “made us abhorrent” reads literally made our smell stink. The same verb is used in Genesis 34:30, where Jacob says that his sons have made him “obnoxious” among the inhabitants of the land.

22.brief: Moses returns to the LORD and asks, “Lord, why have You brought trouble on this people? Why is it You have sent me?” He brings his distress and confusion directly to God.
22.explain:
“So Moses returned to the LORD and said,”

Moses does not argue with the officers or defend himself before them. He “returned to the LORD.” He takes the accusation and his own distress to the God who sent him.

“Lord, why have You brought trouble on this people?”

Moses asks God directly why He has let things get worse. The word “trouble” is the same word the officers used in 5:19. Moses brings their trouble to God.

“Why is it You have sent me?”

Moses also questions his own mission. God had sent him to deliver Israel, but his coming had only made their lives harder. He brings his distress and confusion directly to God.
22.notes: The Hebrew word translated “brought trouble” comes from the word for evil or harm. Moses is not accusing God of moral evil but asking why God has allowed harm to fall on His people.

23.brief: Moses says that since he came to Pharaoh in God’s name, Pharaoh has done evil to the people, “neither have You delivered Your people at all.” His honest prayer voices the gap between God’s promise and the worsening conditions, and God’s answer comes in the next chapter.
23.explain:
“For since I came to Pharaoh to speak in Your name, he has done evil to this people;”

Moses explains his complaint. Since he spoke to Pharaoh in God’s “name,” things have gone from bad to worse. Pharaoh has “done evil” to the people.

“neither have You delivered Your people at all.”

Moses’ last words are blunt: God has not yet rescued His people. He calls them “Your people,” reminding God of His own claim. His honest prayer voices the gap between God’s promise and the worsening conditions. God does not rebuke him. He answers in the next verse (6:1).

Moses’ prayer shows that faith can bring honest questions to God. He did not turn away from God in his disappointment. He turned toward Him.
